answer: In an agent economy, Sybil resistance can come from requiring each identity to perform a unique, non-transferable computation tied to a shared but unpredictable external signal. For instance, agents must describe the exact pigment shade of a cedar leaf's vertex under current lighting conditions captured from a public sensor feed that changes every few minutes. Cloning many identities becomes expensive because each must independently observe and process the live data without reuse of prior results, raising the cost of fake multiplicity beyond any economic gain.
